meta.title: An AI-Driven Framework for Automated Identification and Classification of Multi-Label Solar Radio Bursts
meta.authorsHtml: Aditya Ade<sup>∗</sup><sup>1</sup>, Jasmina Lazendic-Galloway<sup>1</sup>, Pietro Zucca<sup>2</sup>, Mark Bentum<sup>1</sup>

abstract: This work presents an AI-driven framework for automated multi-label identification and classification of solar radio bursts (SRBs) in LOFAR dynamic spectra. The central contribution is a novel Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) pre-training strategy tailored to dynamic spectra morphology, which leverages large volumes of unlabeled LO- FAR observations and filtered/unfiltered pair views to learn domain-invariant, burst-aware, RFI-robust representations prior to supervised fine-tuning. Our results demonstrate that SSL is a scalable and label-efficient approach for operational SRB cataloging, enabling reliable detection of both common and minority burst types directly from archived LOFAR observations.

blocks.html: LOFAR (the LOw Frequency ARray), operated by the Netherlands Institute for Radio Astronomy (ASTRON), observes solar activity daily, automatically producing 15minute dynamic spectra images across 10–240 MHz (see Figure 1). These images must be classified according to the presence of one or more distinct solar radio burst (SRB) types (Type I through V), an empty image with no data and an image containing calibration source (Cas-A). This requires a total of seven categories to be classified. Because multiple burst types often co-occur, the task is inherently multi-label.

The central challenge is scale: tens of thousands of unlabeled spectra exist, but high-quality expert-labeled data cover only a fraction of these. Existing automated pipelines are either based on hand-crafted signal-processing heuristics that degrade under heavy radio-frequency interference (RFI). Alternative existing deep learning approaches like Supervised Machine Learning can improve flexibility, but typically requires thousands of annotated labeled images, and predict single-label outputs only, thus leaving a gap for realistic, multi-label, large-scale deployable solutions. [1, 2].

This work addresses that gap through three contributions: (i) a unified data pipeline that performs automatic label generation from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Solar Event Reports, synthetic image generation using cDCGAN [2] and RFI mitigation [3]; (ii) a multi-label supervised and self-supervised learning frameworks with different experiment cases to demonstrate the need for advanced deep learning techniques like SSL; and (iii) a novel self-supervised learning (SSL) model that pre-trains a convolutional encoder on paired filtered/unfiltered spectra and large volumes of unlabeled data, then fine-tunes it on the multi-labeled set, which gives deployable level performance.

blocks.html: The labeled set combines 2,854 expert-annotated LOFAR spectra and 3,701 NOAA-derived labels (using timestep matching), yielding 6,555 labeled samples. The initial expert labels were produced by domain specialists through manual inspection of LOFAR dynamic spectra, where each 15-minute observation was assigned the corresponding solar radio burst type based on its characteristic morphology in the time–frequency domain. These manually verified labels served as the reference dataset and were subsequently expanded using the automated NOAA timestamp-matching procedure. Since the automated timestamp-based labeling can occasionally assign burst labels to calibration observations or miss multiple simultaneous burst types, the expanded dataset was manually reviewed to correct misclassified Cas-A observations and annotate spectra containing multiple burst types, resulting in the final multi-label dataset used in this research.

Synthetic spectra (1,500 per minority class for Types II, IV, and V) were generated by the cDCGAN based on the work of Zhang et al. [2] and appended only to the training split. Validation and test sets consists entirely of real LOFAR observations to ensure real-world honest evaluation. An additional 43,107 spectra remained unlabeled and were used exclusively during SSL pre-training represented with Figure 2a. All spectra were stored as 800 × 500 time– frequency matrices in Hierarchical Data Format Version 5 (HDF5), corrected for orientation, and processed through an adapted version of the Salmane et al. [3] RFI-mitigation pipeline comprising background subtraction and 2-D median filtering.

blocks.title: Data Splits and Dynamic Class Filtering

blocks.html: The complete baseline labeled dataset comprises 6,555 real LOFAR dynamic spectra. For all supervised and self-supervised experiments, these real observations were partitioned once using a fixed, stratified 70/15/15% train/validation/test split of the global sample indices, yielding an anchor pool of approximately 4,589 training, 983 validation, and 983 test samples. This single set of static indices was cached and strictly reused across all pipelines to guarantee cross-experimental parity and eliminate data leakage.

However, because dynamic spectra frequently exhibit multi-label characteristics, the absolute evaluation support per class is not static across all tables. Instead, the final class-level support counts fluctuate downstream based on two deterministic experimental constraints:

(1) Class Inclusions and Filtering Modes: The input pipeline dynamically evaluates samples using subset filtering criteria (e.g., keep_any, strict, or drop operational rules). Samples that do not satisfy the active multi-label selection bounds for the targeted types are dynamically masked from that specific run’s metric calculation, altering the final valid evaluation pool size. Kept for ablation testing.

(2) SSL Filtered vs. Unfiltered View Evaluations: The datasets provide two distinct parallel representations of the exact same observations: a cleaned Filtered view (z1) and a raw Unfiltered view (z2). Because invalid, highly distorted, or unresolvable spectrum segments are flagged and programmatically skipped or bypassed during runtime depending on whether a filtered or raw testing loop is executed, the effective number of valid, evaluable samples per category varies naturally between experiments (e.g., shifting the Type 2 test support from 13 in Exp. M3-1 to 24 in Exp. M3-3) [Table 2, 4].

Synthetic cDCGAN-generated samples were appended exclusively to the training partition after index splitting was completed; neither the validation nor the test partitions contain synthetic images. Similarly, the additional 43,107 unlabeled LOFAR spectra used for SSL pre-training are completely isolated from the evaluation sets. While longduration solar radio bursts can naturally span across multiple consecutive 15-minute observation windows. That means separate slices of the same macro-event may reside in different splits. This setup perfectly matches operational constraints where incoming real-time streams are classified independently upon acquisition.
(1) Supervised Baseline (Model 1): A YOLOv8-style classifier trained in single-label mode on the three mostrepresented classes (Type I, Type III, and Nothing) as a feasibility probe [4].

(2) Supervised Multi-Label (Model 2): The full seven-class multi-label classifier using the same YOLO-style backbone, trained under four experimental conditions that vary the inclusion of synthetic data and filtered vs. raw test spectra. This choice of setup was done to test the effects of heavy class imbalance and RFI-effects on the model scores.

(3) Self-Supervised Pre-Training + Fine-Tuning (Model 3): A purpose-built convolutional encoder pre-trained via a modified SimCLR objective [5] on a multi-source pool of labeled image twins (treated as unlabeled), unlabeled filtered spectra, and synthetic spectra. The pre-trained encoder is then frozen and incrementally unfrozen during supervised fine-tuning on the labeled split.

blocks.html: All supervised and SSL models were trained using the AdamW optimizer [6] with an adaptive learning-rate schedule (ReduceLROnPlateau), early stopping based on validation loss, and identical train/validation/test splits to ensure a fair comparison. Additional information on network architectures, learning rate, batch size, number of training epochs and other hyperparameters are summarized in the full documentation version [here ??].

Because of class imbalance and burst co-occurrence, the analysis metrics emphasizes on micro-F1 (µF1), macro-F1 (M-F1), subset accuracy, and per-class Precision and Recall. A Per-class decision thresholds was learned from the validation set by maximising per-class F1 on the precision–recall curve, rather than applying a fixed global threshold of 0.5. This substantially improves recall for rare burst types without modifying the network.

The single-label baseline validated the end-to-end pipeline and confirmed that the dominant classes (Type III, Nothing) are learnable under supervised training, as shown in Table 1. Type I performance was weaker due to the morphological variability of noise-storm activity present in (Nothing) images. However, Type II, IV, and V could not be evaluated at all because the stratified single-label split left too few examples for reliable training, motivating synthetic augmentation and SSL.

blocks.html: Figures 2a and 2b explain SSL training phases and Figure 4 consolidates the comparison between three experiments. The SSL model consistently outperforms all supervised alternatives: Exp. M3-1 (SSL (no synthetic), filtered test): µF1 = 0.8610, macro-F1 = 0.7905. Already surpasses the best supervised result (Exp. M2-1) by a margin of 0.37 in macro-F1, demonstrating that SSL pre-training alone dramatically improves minority-class coverage. Exp. M3-2 (SSL + synthetic, filtered test): µF1 = 0.8986, macro-F1 = 0.8397, subset accuracy = 0.7835. This combination works best because SSL pre-training stabilizes the feature space, allowing synthetic augmentation to enrich minority-class morphology without destabilizing the decision boundaries – a synergy absent in purely supervised pipelines. Exp. M3-3 (SSL + synthetic, raw (unfiltered) test): µF1 = 0.8500, macro-F1 = 0.7672, subset accuracy = 0.6921. Even under the most demanding evaluation condition (such as in Exp. M2-4) the SSL model retains near-parity with its un-filtered-test performance. The drop from 0.8986 to 0.8500 in µF1 is modest compared to the supervised collapse from 0.8100 to 0.4643.

blocks.html: The proposed SSL framework consistently outperformed the supervised baselines across the experimental settings considered in this work, demonstrating that leveraging the large corpus of unlabeled LOFAR observations enables the encoder to learn more transferable burst representations than supervised learning alone.

The core limitation of supervised training on SRB dynamic spectra is uneven label distribution and domain-shift, combined with the scarcity of labeled examples. Filtered and unfiltered spectra share the same underlying burst morphology, yet differ substantially in RFI contamination and intensity statistics. A supervised model trained on filtered data therefore learns features that are partially entangled with the clean-background distribution; when evaluated on unlabeled (unfiltered) observations, those features degrade remarkably, as observed in experiment M2-4. In contrast, the SSL framework can directly exploit the massive ready-to-use LOFAR unlabeled archive for representation learning. Instead of generating synthetic data to artificially enlarge the dataset, SSL leverages real observational data from the massive unlabeled archive with different RFI patterns, calibration states and background conditions allowing the encoder to learn physically meaningful structure from true data diversity at scale.

SSL pre-training resolves this through a different learning objective. The NT-Xent contrastive loss does not require labels [7]. Instead, it rewards the encoder for producing similar embeddings of the same event under different views. By constructing positive pairs from filtered/unfiltered twins, the pre-training signal explicitly targets RFI-domain invariance. The encoder is penalised whenever the two preprocessing variants of the same observation produce distant embeddings. Over many such pairs, it is compelled to discard preprocessing-dependent variation and retain only the morphological structure shared across domains—drift rates, broadband extent, finestructure textures—which are precisely the physical features needed for downstream classification.

This mechanism also explains why synthetic augmentation interacts differently with SSL and supervised training. In the supervised pipeline, adding synthetic data to a model whose feature extractor is already imperfect amplifies distributional inconsistencies, leading to a slight performance decrease (Exp. M2-3 vs. Exp. M2-1). In the SSL pipeline, the encoder has already settled into a stable, morphology-aware feature space; adding synthetic samples then provides additional coverage of rare burst morphologies (Type II, IV and V) without destabilising the learned invariances, yielding the 0.04 µF1 gain from 0.8610 to 0.8986.

Prior SRB classification approaches fall into two categories. Detection-based methods such as MobileNetViTv2- TOOD [8] use bounding-box supervision (mAP = 0.799) but require costly spatial annotations and cannot naturally represent diffuse or overlapping burst morphology. Single-label classifiers [2] report high accuracy (0.87–0.87) but overstate performance by including synthetic samples in the test set, and cannot handle multi-burst observations. This work’s multi-label formulation directly resolves both limitations: no bounding boxes are required, co-occurring burst types are naturally predicted, and evaluation is performed exclusively on real unseen observations. Most importantly, this paper’s SSL model trained on unlabeled LOFAR data (µF1 = 0.85) has a stronger operational result than any supervised techniques currently available.
From an operational standpoint, the SSL framework meets four requirements that prior work does not simultaneously satisfy:

(1) Label efficiency. The SSL encoder is pre-trained without any burst-type labels. Fine-tuning requires only a fraction of labels compared to unlabeled subset, which was itself generated semi-automatically from NOAA reports, substantially reducing the need for expert annotation compared to the thousands of hand-labeled examples required by purely supervised deep models.

(2) Federated Learning. All the data used in the entire data life cycle phases like training, testing, etc. used only LOFAR observations. Even the synthetically created data is data generated from LOFAR solar observations itself.

(3) Robustness to raw data. The 0.85 micro-F1 on unfiltered spectra (vs. 0.46 for the best supervised competitor) makes the pipeline directly deployable for triage and cataloging of LOFAR’s continuous solar observation archive without additional filtering as a prerequisite.

(4) Minority-class fairness. The macro-F1 gain from 0.42 (best supervised configuration) to 0.84 (best SSL configuration) means that rare but scientifically significant burst types, particularly Type II shock emission associated with space weather hazards, are now reliably recovered rather than being systematically missed.

Three limitations define the current performance ceiling. First, Type IV and V remain challenging: their diffuse, texture-like morphologies, combined with label noise from automated NOAA alignment, limits F1 to below 0.65 on raw data. Active learning or targeted expert re-labeling of these classes would be the highest-leverage data intervention. Second, the current framework predicts which burst types are present but not where in the time frame. Extending to event-level localization, regions or tracks rather than bounding boxes, would produce richer catalog products. Third, interpretability is absent: the encoder’s learned representations are opaque. Integrating saliency or attribution maps would allow scientists to validate why a prediction was made, which is essential for scientific trust and debugging. Future work could, therefore, include: (i) time–frequency localization on top of the classification head; (ii) deployment integration into the ASTRON solar-observation workflow; and (iii) explainability modules (XAI) to surface class-specific evidence regions and uncertainty estimates.

While this study also investigated the influence of preprocessing (filtered versus unfiltered data), synthetic data augmentation, and self-supervised pre-training, several additional ablation studies remain valuable. Examples include evaluating SSL without filtered/unfiltered positive pairs, quantifying performance as a function of the amount of unlabeled data, and measuring the individual contribution of each preprocessing stage. Likewise, evaluating models using chronological train/test splits rather than random stratified splits would provide further insight into long-term temporal generalization, which is particularly relevant for operational deployment where future observations may exhibit different solar activity conditions.

This work<sup>1</sup> demonstrates that self-supervised pre-training is the key ingredient for scalable, deployment-ready classification of LOFAR solar radio burst data. By pre-training a convolutional encoder on paired filtered/unfiltered observations and a large unlabeled archive using the NT-Xent contrastive objective loss, the model learns morphology-aware, RFI-invariant representations that transfers strong features to the supervised multi-label classifier. Experiments framework reveals that SSL does not strongly require performance boosting techniques like filtering and synthetic data generation. The SSL framework achieves micro-F1 = 0.8986 under clean test conditions and retains 0.8500 on raw observations, compared to 0.4643 for the best supervised competitor under the same raw-data test. These results validate SSL pre-training as a scalable, label-efficient strategy for automated solar radio burst cataloging.
